text: Everything covered in this cluster so far answers the same question -- what happens when two transactions might touch the same data at the same time -- with one of two fundamentally different philosophies: pessimistic, or optimistic.

Pessimistic concurrency assumes conflicts are likely, and prevents them up front by blocking other sessions before a conflict can even occur. That's every locking-based level: READ UNCOMMITTED, READ COMMITTED, REPEATABLE READ, and SERIALIZABLE, each just drawing the line for how much to block in a different place.

Optimistic concurrency assumes conflicts are rare, and lets every session proceed without blocking anyone -- only dealing with a conflict if one actually happens, at the moment of writing. SNAPSHOT is the clearest example: it never blocks a reader or a writer, it just detects the rare write-write conflict afterward and makes the second writer retry.

The same optimistic idea shows up outside the database engine entirely, as an application pattern using a rowversion column. The application reads a row's value and its RowVer together, then updates conditionally on that same RowVer still matching. If someone else updated the row in between, the update affects zero rows, and the application knows to reload and retry.

So the trade-off is symmetric. Pessimistic locking costs unnecessary blocking when conflicts turn out to be rare. Optimistic approaches cost frequent retries and wasted work when conflicts turn out to be frequent. Neither one is free -- they're just paying the cost at a different point.
Next lesson, the capstone of this whole cluster: putting all six isolation levels into one practical decision framework, so you know which one to actually reach for on the job. See you there.
